newsitem.title: USA: Policy group pushes US environmental rule changes.
newsitem.headline: Policy group pushes US environmental rule changes.

text.p: An environmental policy group Monday laid out a plan to tackle all kinds of pollution under one statute, and avoid the fragmented approach of laws targeted at specific types of pollution.

The National Environmental Policy Institute report suggested how the nation can move to a "unified statute" to oversee major forms of pollution -- air, water and soil -- and prevent polluters from shifting emissions to avoid the strictest rules.
The plan also would give more discretion to states and industries to decide how environmental standards would be met.
"The existing system in too many cases has evolved into a bureaucratic gridlock that precludes the active participation of stakeholders in environmental problem-solving," it said.
The report by members of industry, academia, the environmental community and government recommended making the switch to unified standards in two stages.

In the first phase, the Environmental Protection Agency would authorize states to issue facility-wide permits covering all pollution forms and giving industries power to use new approaches as long as they meet standards and give more environmental benefits.
In the next phase, while the EPA would still set standards, states would have greater flexibility in selecting the best strategies to meet them.
The EPA would revise standards in the Clean Water Act, the Clean Air Act and the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act to make them consistent.
While the report said the EPA should have leeway on how to carry out the changes, the EPA should give states more responsiblity to meet goals and should be less involved in how they do it.
"If we are to substantively change the 'one-size-fits-all' paradigm, greater trust in the commitment and competency of the states must occur," it said.
The report also said the United States must shift quickly toward these changes as Europe already is moving toward them.

"If we fail to move in this direction, and do so quickly, we will no longer be seen as a leader in environmental management, but a follower -- saddled with an outmoded, inefficient and expensive approach to environmental management that will result in a competitive disadvantage," it said.
